doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: Understanding the Nazi threat; his father the writer
summary: As a child he grasped why they left; he recalls Nazi labour gangs, his father losing his newspaper job, and his father's friendship with Alban Berg.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Can you recall, as an 8-year-old, understanding why you had to leave the country?

Oh yes. I understood that. I mean I didn’t understand it on a very highly sophisticated level, but I absolutely knew — we still didn’t know at that time — that was before the Holocaust really, it was before — 1942 was really when that really evil stuff — but it was bad enough as it was. I remember even before, when I was about six or so, one of my aunts had a boyfriend who was — this was at my grandmother’s place — and like © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

everybody of a certain age there, he was forced into doing stuff for the government. And he was actually in a kind of labor gang, not full time, but they were working on building the famous Autobahn. And he had to wear a kind of uniform thing with a swastika armband. And I remember him arriving at my grandmother’s and tearing off this thing and throwing it in a corner and saying, you know, as if it was something dirty. He left very soon after. He wanted my aunt to come with him. He went to Australia. He immigrated to Australia. So he was a non-Jewish — he was an Arian anti-Nazi. And there was conversation, you know, pretty constant, about what the Nazis represented. My father was a writer. He had been a Viennese cultural correspondent for a major German newspaper in Frankfurt, which actually was started by my great-great grandfather. And so once the Nazis took over the paper was Jewish-owned, but, you know, they were stripped of it and my father lost his job. My father had been born in what was then the Austria Hungarian Empire, but later, after World War I became Poland, now it’s Ukraine, you know, it’s right on the border there. But my father was born actually not even in what they call a shtetl, which is like a little village, but he was born in the country, out in the country. But he was born into a religious Jewish family. They were Hasidm, so he was raised that way. And then of course he went to Vienna to study and he became a cosmopolitan so to speak. He was a great music lover. He had played cello as a young man in his school orchestra. He actually became the first cellist. But he’d given that up. But he became a close friend of Alban Berg so I remember Berg, who died when I was just six years old. But I remember him well because he was a close friend, and sometimes my father and he would take me to — well they were soccer fans and would go to soccer games.
